metadata.title: De Buono v. NYSA-ILA Medical and Clinical Services Fund, 520 U.S. 806 (1997) (No. 95-1594)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: De Buono v. NYSA-ILA Medical and Clinical Services Fund

Opinion filed: 1997-06-02

Docket No.: 95-1594

Citations:
• 138 L. Ed. 2d 21
• 117 S. Ct. 1747
• 520 U.S. 806
• 1997 U.S. LEXIS 3397

Case holding summaries:
• utiliz- ing the “objectives” principle from Travelers and Dillingham
• collecting Supreme Court ERISA preemption cases and documenting the enormous volume of cases in the lower federal courts
• generally applicable gross receipts tax on health care 17 facilities not preempted despite some bur den on administration of ERISA plans
• no preemption of patient services tax
• upholding a state tax on gross receipts for patient services at hospi- tals, residential healthcare facilities, and diagnostic and treatment cen- ters
• ERISA pre-empted state law requiring the provision of pregnancy benefits
• "Section 2(c)(2) of the District's Equity Amendment Act specifically refers to welfare benefit plans regulated by ERISA and on that basis alone is pre-empted"
• "Whatever the purpose or purposes of the New Jersey statute, we conclude that it `relate[s] to pension plans' governed by ERISA because it eliminates one method for calculating pension benefitsintegrationthat is permitted by federal law"
• law that required benefit plans to include minimum mental health benefits "related to" ERISA plans
• generally applicable garnishment law not pre-empted
• a provision that explicitly refers to ERISA in defining the scope of the state law's application is pre-empted
• state law requiring one-time severance payment not pre-empted
• the historic police powers of 9 the State include the regulation of matters of health and safety
• discussing "relate to" language of Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974
• “Any state tax, or other law, that increases the cost of providing benefits to covered employees will have some effect on the administration of ERISA plans, but that simply cannot mean that every state law with such an effect is preempted by the federal statute.”
• applying a presumption that "Congress does not intend to supplant state law"; internal citation omitted
• concluding that ERISA did not pre-empt a state tax on gross receipts for patient services that simply increased the cost of providing benefits
• holding that ERISA did not preempt a New York state tax on the 46 gross receipts of health care facilities operated by an ERISA fund
• no ERISA pre-emption of New York tax law which imposed surcharge on gross receipts of health facilities
• "[T]he historic police powers * * * include the regulation of matters of health and safety."
• “Any state tax, or other law, that increases the cost of providing benefits to covered employees will have some effect on the administration of ERISA plans, but that simply cannot mean that every state law with such an effect is preempted by the federal statute.”
• holding that ERISA did not preempt a New York state tax on the gross receipts of health care facilities operated by an ERISA fund
• "There is nothing in the operation of [this state tax] that convinces us it is the type of state law that Congress intended ERISA to supersede"
• holding that "hospitals operated by ERISA plans are subject to the same laws as other hospitals"
• holding state law "imposing a gross receipts tax on the income of medical centers" not pre-empted as applied to centers "operated by ERISA funds"
• suggesting impact of increased rates for beneficiaries or more limited range of covered services does not justify preemption
• generally applicable gross receipts tax on health care facilities not preempted despite some burden on administration of ERISA plans
• finding gross receipts tax not preempted
• “In Travelers . . . . we were quite clear . . . that the text could not be read to ‘extend to the furthest stretch of its indeterminacy’ . . . .” (quoting Travelers, 514 U.S. at 655)
